overview: Mbanza Kongo was a political and spiritual capital whose built landscape combined royal institutions, sacred places and Christian churches. Engagement with Portugal changed religious and literary life without simply replacing Kongo customs.

items.text: A bilingual Portuguese and Kikongo catechism was published in 1624, part of a wider process of translating Christian concepts into local categories.
Stone churches joined an existing settlement built from local materials. The royal residence, customary court and sacred places remained central to urban identity.
Kongo crucifixes reworked Christian imagery through local visual conventions. Their precise dates and places of manufacture often remain uncertain.
Kimpa Vita's Antonian movement began in 1704 and called for the restoration of Kongo's unity through a distinctly local Christian message.
Mbanza Kongo retains customary and sacred functions, including institutions through which communities transmit royal memory.

sources.title: The Met: Christianity and Kongo Visual Culture
